Lecture 9: Derived Distributions

Author

Jamie Haddock

Derived Distributions

The Two-Step Process

We want the PDF of \(Y = g(X)\) for a continuous RV \(X\) with known PDF \(f_X\).

Step 1. Find the CDF of \(Y\): \[F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y) = P(g(X) \le y) = \int_{\{x \mid g(x) \le y\}} f_X(x)dx\] by translating the event \(\{g(X)\le y\}\) into an event about \(X\) and using \(f_X\) to compute its probability.

Step 2. Differentiate: \[f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy} F_Y(y)\]

Why not go directly PMF-style? In the discrete case, if \(g\) is invertible we can write \(p_Y(y) = p_X(g^{-1}(y))\) directly. We need to go through the Fundamental Law of Calculus/differentiate the CDF route because we can only say that the mass of events are equal, not the density!

Example: \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), \(Y = \sqrt{X}\)

\[F_Y(y) = P(\sqrt X \le y) = P(X \le y^2) = y^2, \qquad 0 \le y \le 1\]

\[f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}\, y^2 = 2y, \qquad 0 \le y \le 1\]

Linear Case: \(Y = aX + b\)

Applying the two-step process for \(a > 0\): \[F_Y(y) = P(aX + b \le y) = P\Big(X \le \frac{y-b}{a}\Big) = F_X\Big(\frac{y-b}{a}\Big)\]

Differentiating (chain rule), and handling \(a<0\) the same way, gives the general formula: \[f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{|a|}\, f_X\Big(\frac{y-b}{a}\Big)\]

Example: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), \(Y = aX + b\)

Plugging the Normal PDF into the linear-case formula gives \[f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{|a|\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\frac{y-b}{a}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)\] which is exactly the \(\mathcal{N}(a\mu + b,\; a^2\sigma^2)\) density.

We saw this previously, using the PDF of a monotonic function of a RV theorem!

Exercise

Exercise

\(X\) is Exponential(\(\lambda\)), and \(Y = aX + b\) with \(a > 0\).

  • What is the PDF of \(Y\)?
  • Is \(Y\) exponential?

Exercise – Solution

For \(a>0\): \(x = \frac{y-b}{a} \ge 0 \iff y \ge b\), so \[f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{a} \lambda\, e^{-\lambda (y-b)/a}, \qquad y \ge b\] \[F_Y(y) = 1 - e^{-\lambda (y-b)/a}, \qquad y \ge b\]

Is \(Y\) exponential? Only if \(b = 0\) – then \(Y \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda/a)\) exactly. If \(b \ne 0\), \(Y\) has the exponential shape but shifted to start at \(b\) instead of \(0\): it’s memoryless from \(b\) onward, not from \(0\), so it is not itself an Exponential random variable.

(If \(a<0\) instead, the same formula applies but the support flips to \(y \le b\).)

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
lam, a = 0.5, 2.0

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for b, color in [(0.0, "C0"), (3.0, "C3")]:
    X = rng.exponential(1 / lam, 200_000)
    Y = a * X + b
    y = np.linspace(b, Y.max(), 400)
    fy = (lam / a) * np.exp(-lam * (y - b) / a)
    ax.hist(Y, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.35, color=color)
    label = r"$b=0$: exactly Exponential($\lambda/a$)" if b == 0 else r"$b=3$: shifted, not Exponential"
    ax.plot(y, fy, color=color, lw=2, label=label)

ax.set_title(r"$Y = aX+b$ for $X\sim\mathrm{Exponential}(\lambda)$")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Recall: Monotonic Case

The linear case generalizes: if \(g\) is strictly monotonic and differentiable, with inverse \(h = g^{-1}\), \[f_Y(y) = f_X(h(y))\, |h'(y)|\]

Specializing to \(g(x) = ax+b\): \(h(y) = \frac{y-b}{a}\), \(h'(y) = \frac{1}{a}\), recovering exactly the linear-case formula above.

Review of Proof

The formula follows from the same two-step process, using that monotonicity lets us rewrite the event \(\{g(X) \le y\}\) as an event about \(X\) alone: \[\{g(X) \le y\} = \{X \le h(y)\}\] if \(g\) is increasing, or \(\{X \ge h(y)\}\) if \(g\) is decreasing.

Functions of Two Random Variables

Same two-step process applies: For \(Z = g(X,Y)\), jointly continuous \(X,Y\):

Step 1. \(F_Z(z) = P(g(X,Y) \le z) = \displaystyle\iint_{\{(x,y)\,:\,g(x,y)\le z\}} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx\,dy\)

Step 2. \(f_Z(z) = \dfrac{d}{dz} F_Z(z)\)

The only new wrinkle is that “the event” is now a region of the plane rather than an interval of the line.

Example: \(X, Y \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) independent, \(Z = Y/X\)

\(\{Z \le z\} = \{Y \le zX\}\): the region of the unit square below the line \(y = zx\). Its area looks different depending on whether the line exits through the top of the square or the right edge.

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5))

for ax, z, title in [(axes[0], 0.5, "z < 1: line exits the right edge"),
                      (axes[1], 2.0, "z >= 1: line exits the top edge")]:
    xx = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
    yy = np.clip(z * xx, 0, 1)
    ax.fill_between(xx, 0, yy, color="C0", alpha=0.4)
    ax.plot(xx, np.clip(z * xx, 0, 1.3), color="C0", lw=2, label=f"y = {z}x")
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title(f"z = {z}\n{title}")
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
    ax.set_ylabel("y")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Integrating the shaded area in each case: \[F_Z(z) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{z}{2} & 0 \le z < 1 \\[4pt] 1 - \dfrac{1}{2z} & z \ge 1 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f_Z(z) = \begin{cases} \dfrac12 & 0 < z < 1 \\[4pt] \dfrac{1}{2z^2} & z \ge 1 \end{cases}\]

Sanity check: \(\int_0^1 \frac12\,dz + \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{2z^2}\,dz = \frac12+\frac12=1\). \(\checkmark\)

Sums of Random Variables – Convolution

Motivation: the Discrete Case

For independent discrete RVs \(X, Y\) and \(Z = X+Y\): \[ \begin{aligned} p_Z(z) &= P(X + Y = z) \\&= \sum_{\{(x,y) \mid x+y = z\}}P(X=x, Y=y) \\&= \sum_x P(X=x, Y = z-x) \\&=\sum_x p_X(x)\, p_Y(z-x) \end{aligned} \]

We sum over every way \(x\) and \(z-x\) could combine to produce the total \(z\). This is the convolution of \(p_X\) and \(p_Y\).

The Continuous Case

Replacing sums with integrals: for independent continuous \(X,Y\), \[F_Z(z) = P(X+Y\le z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\, F_Y(z-x)\, dx\] Differentiating in \(z\) gives the continuous convolution formula: \[f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\, f_Y(z-x)\, dx\]

Example: Sum of i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) RVs

Suppose \(X, Y \sim \text{Uniform}([0,1])\) are independent. The PDF of \(Z = X + Y\) is \[f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)dx.\] The integrand is nonzero (equal to 1) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) and \(0 \le z-x \le 1\).

Combining these, we see the integrand is nonzero for \(\max\{0,z-1\} \le x \le \min\{1,z\}\). Thus, \[f_Z(z) = \min\{1,z\} - \max\{0,z-1\} \text{ for } 0 \le z \le 2.\]

Example: Sum of Independent Normal RVs is Normal

If \(X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)\), \(Y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)\) independent, then \[X+Y \sim \mathcal N(\mu_1+\mu_2,\ \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\]

Sketch Plugging both Gaussian densities into \(f_Z(z)=\int f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)\,dx\) gives an integrand of the form \(\exp(-(\text{quadratic in } x))\); completing the square in \(x\) separates the integral into a constant (in \(x\)) factor times a Gaussian integral over \(x\) that evaluates to \(1\). What’s left as a function of \(z\) is exactly the \(\mathcal N(\mu_1+\mu_2,\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\) density.

Graphical Calculation of Convolutions

\(f_Z(z) = \int f_X(x)\, f_Y(z-x)\, dx\) has a picture: flip \(f_Y\) about the vertical axis, slide it by \(z\), multiply pointwise against \(f_X\), and the shaded overlap area is \(f_Z(z)\).
